ML-015: Creoleana was written by a white Barbadian who lived through the era of slavery, and it looks back fondly on island society in those years. Its love story takes place in a world built on the forced labour of enslaved Africans, whose own voices the book largely leaves out. We include it because it is one of the earliest Barbadian novels, but it is a view from one side of a deeply unequal society.
ML-146: James Grainger was a Scottish doctor who settled on St Kitts, married into a planter family and lived within the plantation economy. His best-known poem, The Sugar-Cane, includes advice on buying and managing enslaved people. This ballad of two lovers comes from that world, and its tenderness sits uneasily beside the cruelty that sustained it.
ML-168: John Gabriel Stedman was a soldier sent to Suriname to fight people who had escaped slavery. His account of Joanna, an enslaved woman, is often read as a love story, but he wrote it as a man with power over her, and her own view of their relationship was never recorded. It is included as an important, and troubling, record of love under slavery.
ML-110: Paul et Virginie was written by a French author who had lived on the island when it was a French colony worked by enslaved people. He criticised slavery in his other writing, yet the story's island idyll still depends on enslaved characters who serve in the background. It became one of the most widely read love stories of its age, and its picture of colonial life should be read with that history in mind.
